(y(0) − yˆ′ for decreasing objectives (“–”),
pi pi
where yˆ′ is the property value achieved by the manipulated molecule and y(0) is that of the source molecule. By this definition, more positive improvement is always preferred regardless of the manipulation direction.

We report “success” cases where (1) the generated molecule is valid and novel (not observed in the training set; Fig. S8); (2) the 3D Tanimoto similarity between the generated molecule and the source is greater than 0.5 (95% quantile of random pairwise similarity; Fig. S7); (3) all properties have improvements above a given threshold, where σ is the standard deviation of the property p . We use either a relaxed (>0) or strict (>0.5σ ) improvement threshold. Fig. 3A demonstrates that MolDiffdAE-based methods perform significantly better than the baselines in all but one task, especially under strict improvement thresholds. Furthermore, fine-tuning, back-propagation manipulation and RAG, when applicable, could enhance the overall performance, especially on the more complex properties (QED, SAS, LogP). Meanwhile, the majority of the compositional and structural patterns are well preserved as the manipulated molecules remain similar to their sources qualitatively (Fig. 3C,D,E, I; Fig. S10A). We also show that our methods achieve better numerical preservation of the irrelevant molecular properties, especially with fine-tuning and RAG (Fig. 3B; see Methods for more details).

A detailed analysis of the improvements shows that MolDiffdAE-manipulated molecules generally achieve a better trade-off between all objectives, while classifier guidance occasionally succeeds in one objective but fails in the others (Fig. 3D, F, H; Fig. S10B). These results highlight the advantage of MolDiffdAE’s well-regularized and disentangled latent space, as the objectives have minimal interference with each other. We also observe that the 2D graph-based VAE achieves reasonable success in manipulating the target properties (Table S7), but fails to preserve the 3D similarity, leading to lower final performance. MolDiffdAE, on the other hand, could better preserve both the composition and shape due to the strong semantic control.

In addition, we also analyze the geometric features (Table S4) and conformer energy (Fig. S5A) of the generated molecules, where MolDiffdAE-based methods, especially when combined with classifier back-propagation and RAG, display higher generation quality, indicating a well-regularized latent semantic space that facilitates smooth exploration. In the following sections, we provide a more comprehensive and in-depth analysis of MolDiffdAE’s controlled generation capacity, by investigating its manipulation behavior regarding molecular fragments, preservation of 3D shapes and protein interactions, and ability to manipulate 3D properties.

Case study 1: Joint manipulation of LogP and SAS
We perform an in-depth comparison between the manipulation results targeting both lower LogP (higher water solubility) and lower SAS (higher synthetic accessibility) for MolDiffdAE-based manipulation and classifier guidance. These properties are ideal targets for evaluating the impact of the disentangled latent space, as both of them are defined by the combined contribution of the molecular fragments: LogP is calculated as the sum of the hydrophilicity score of each atom [53], and SAS based on the frequencies of the fragments, as more common fragments imply easier synthesis [54]. As a result, different fragments may have aligned or diverging impacts on LogP and SAS. Thus, it is important for the property manipulation process to separate their differential contributions, and introduce fragments that contribute to both objectives.

In the first example (Fig. 4A), classifier guidance successfully reduces the SAS score by replacing the low accessibility backbone with a high accessibility one. However, some of these newly introduced fragments also reduce water solubility. For example, additional benzene rings are highly accessible but less water-soluble. Similarly, in Fig. 4B, the low accessibility backbone is modified, but solubility is not improved as the new backbone does not include more hydrophilic atoms. In comparison, manipulation with MolDiffdAE successfully considers both objectives, as it introduces fragments that are both more synthetically accessible and more water-soluble.

We further complicate the task by adding “more halogens” as another objective. This objective could interfere with the reduction of LogP as halogens are hydrophobic. Meanwhile, aromatic carbons bound to halogens would slightly increase water solubility as a result of the polarization of the aromatic ring. We show that on top of the aforementioned behaviors, MolDiffdAE-based manipulation also tends to attach halogens to aromatic rings to counteract the hydrophobic effect of halogens, while avoiding aliphatic carbons (Fig. 4C, D). In contrast, classifier guidance could trivially succeed in increasing the number of halogens, but fail to make other necessary modifications accordingly to reduce LogP (Fig. 4C) or SAS (Fig. 4D).

These results further prove that the disentangled semantic space successfully guides the diffusion model in multi-objective manipulation tasks. Manipulation in the disentangled semantic embedding space of MolDiffdAE could identify directions that simultaneously satisfy all objectives. With simple classifier guidance, however, the gradient of the classifiers could lead to conflicting directions and interfere with each other without proper regularization.

Case study 2: Validity enhancement by retrieval-augmented generation
We observe that using RAG achieves competitive results with MolDiffdAE-ft+bp, the best-performing method without RAG, in the tasks involving QED, SAS and LogP, and noticeably better results under relaxed improvement thresholds (> 0). A detailed analysis shows comparable performance in terms of success rate (Fig. 3A) and similarity to the source (Fig. 5A, top) between the MolDiffdAE-based methods, while RAG noticeably improves the validity of the generated molecules (Fig. 5A, middle). We also show that the generation quality is overall higher with RAG, in terms of the distribution of geometric properties (Fig. 5A, bottom; Table S4). We notice no significant performance differences between the two RAG methods tested.

Fig. 5B shows that in some of the success cases, the retrieved molecules already contain the desired target properties, due to an information-rich and structured latent space. More importantly, the generated molecule incorporates compositional features from both the source molecule and the retrieved molecule, potentially enhancing the generation quality by keeping the manipulated embedding closer to the data distribution.

External Application 1: Binding-preserving property manipulation
Due to its ability to preserve 3D shapes, which is closely related to the interaction conformations, our semantics-guided property manipulation is particularly useful for protein-binding ligands. In those cases, the binding toward the target protein should be maintained, while some useful properties such as QED, LogP and SAS are modified. To test the generalizability of our method to this task, we apply both our pre-trained and fine-tuned model to the external test set of CrossDocked [55], which contains the 3D structure of 100 ligand-receptor pairs. We observe that MolDiffdAE-based methods show competitive performance with classifier guidance on single-objective tasks (Table S6), and significantly higher performance on multi-objective tasks (Fig. 6A).

We then dock the manipulated molecules back to their respective receptors using QuickVina [56, 57]. Fig. 6B shows examples where the docking is mostly maintained after manipulating the target properties, as reflected by similar docking scores. Overall, on top of successes in improving the target properties, MolDiffdAE-based manipulation could also preserve the Vina score distribution of the source molecules. Meanwhile, classifier guidance preserves the 3D shape and docking but fails in the manipulation objective (Fig. 6A), while 2D VAE-based manipulation breaks the docking (Fig. 6C, D). These results are particularly compelling as our MolDiffdAE model is not explicitly conditioned on the structure of the receptor, but could still maintain the binding throughout the property manipulation. Thus, it could be used to manipulate lead compounds without the need to jointly model both the ligand and the receptor, as the preservation of the 3D shape implicitly preserves the docking. As reliable structures for ligand-receptor complexes are relatively rare, our method could efficiently transfer the 3D shape knowledge from the more data-rich domain of isolated 3D molecules to the generation and manipulation of ligands. It is noteworthy that the method only preserves the 3D shape not necessarily the binding itself, which would require fine-tuning with the protein pocket as the direct conditioning. We leave these for further studies.

External Application 2: Manipulation of DRD2 binding affinity
Beyond basic molecular properties, we further test our method on more complex external properties. We focus on increasing the binding affinity to the dopamine D2 receptor (DRD2). Despite being a well-studied benchmark, the 3D structural data for positive DRD2 binders is still relatively scarce. We select 1400 positive structures from GEOM using the oracle predictor provided by the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) [58]. Due to the complex nature of protein binding, the small data size makes it difficult to train reliable 3D structure-based classifiers or conditioned diffusion models. We fine-tune our MolDiffdAE model on the DRD2 binding dataset, achieving good separation of positives and negatives in the semantic space (Fig. 7A), and perform linear manipulation to increase the binding affinity score. The generated molecules are then evaluated by the same oracle model, and we report positive molecules with binding score >0.5.

As shown in Fig. 7B, MolDiffdAE-ft with linear manipulation outperforms all baselines with a simple one-pass generation and no post-generation filtering. This implies that fine-tuning of the latent semantic space enables efficient use of the limited labeled data. We observe that the manipulated molecules have more hydrophobic components, such as aliphatic carbon (Fig. 7C), naturally resulting in higher LogP (Fig. 7D, bottom). This encourages binding toward DRD2’s highly hydrophobic pocket. Also, though not an explicit objective, the manipulated molecules also show higher QED (Fig. 7D, top), indicating underlying mutual factors that contribute to both DRD2 binding and drug-likeness. However, the manipulation also increases synthetic difficulty (higher SAS; Fig. 7D, middle). This could be potentially improved by jointly manipulating SAS as well, as in previous experiments.

Manipulation of 3D properties
Most of the existing works for controlled molecular generation are restricted to compositional properties, due to their limitations of relying on sequence or 2D graph representations, while the manipulation of 3D geometric properties remains poorly explored. MolDiffdAE as an equivariant 3D diffusion model enables operation on those properties. We manipulate asphericity (Asp) and radius of gyration (RoG) with linear manipulation. As expected, the 2D VAE fails in controlling the 3D properties. Among the 3D equivariant model-based methods, MolDiffdAE shows superior performance in both single- and multi-objective tasks, especially under more stringent improvement thresholds (>0.5σ ) (Fig. 8A).

Contrary to our previous results on compositional properties where the composition undergoes drastic changes while the 3D shape is mostly preserved, manipulation of the 3D properties typically leads to major alterations in the 3D shapes compared to the source molecules (Fig. 8B). In agreement with common observations, molecules with higher asphericity are less spherical, while molecules with higher radius of gyration are more spatially stretched. Meanwhile, the composition of the source is well-preserved after the manipulation. We also observe a good trade-off between the objectives with MolDiffdAE, while classifier guidance either fails in achieving both objectives, or generates few valid molecules (Fig. 8C). The latter suggests the complexity of 3D geometries and implies the usefulness of encoding the 3D structural information into the molecular semantics. Such tasks would be useful in the search of candidate molecules with a preferred 3D shape and a fixed chemical composition.

Discussion
In this study, we present MolDiffdAE, an equivariant diffusion model guided by a disentangled semantic latent space for the controlled generation of 3D molecules. We show that the semantic embedding effectively controls the composition, shape, and molecular properties of the generated molecules, in both stochastic generation and deterministic property manipulation. More importantly, the regularization-induced disentanglement of the semantic embedding empowers effective multi-objective manipulation, which is a challenge for traditional diffusion models where the latent space is entangled and difficult to operate on. Though trained in an unsupervised manner, our pre-trained model is capable of capturing simple compositional and 3D shape properties, and can be used to manipulate them through the semantic embedding. For more complex properties whose contributing factors are distributed across many atoms, such as drug-likeness, solubility, synthetic accessibility and protein binding affinity, we show that our model could be further fine-tuned on small, external property-labeled datasets to enhance the performance.

Several existing controlled molecule generation frameworks on 2D molecules deploy iterative optimization or post-generation filtering to ensure the generation quality and the similarity to the source molecule if required [1, 29]. Our method, however, uses one-pass generation, calling the diffusion decoder only once, and evaluating only the final generation output. Similarity constraint is implicitly enforced by minimizing the distance to the source semantic embedding. Despite the simplified generation pipeline, our method already achieves a good success rate with respect to molecular validity, property values and similarity to the source, as a result of the strong guidance of the semantic embedding and the high capacity of the diffusion model. We also show that the information-rich, low-dimensional semantic embedding vector can be efficiently used for the retrieval of similar molecules and subsequently the enhancement of manipulation results through RAG. Nevertheless, the generation quality of our model could also be further improved through iterative refinement or encoding of the molecular similarity into the latent semantic space with contrastive learning. It is also worth noting that in our experiments, we use randomly sampled “negative” source molecules, some of which may be too challenging for the target value. In real applications, a rational pre-selection of more promising source molecules could further enhance the success rate.

Beyond basic molecular properties, we expect the method to be applicable to a wide spectrum of objectives, such as toxicity, conformational energy, multi-receptor binding affinity, and material properties. It is also possible to associate the semantic embedding with text descriptions, and utilize the recent advances in large language models (LLM) for more flexible conditioning and control [32]. Our framework could also flexibly incorporate recent advances in representation learning and diffusion model architectures for 3D molecules, to enhance the representativeness of the latent space, the quality of generation, and the generalization to rarer and more complex structures. Specifically, using generative models with greater flexibility could enable more drastic manipulations, which is common in real-world drug design and optimization.

Furthermore, although we have demonstrated the preservation of the 3D shape and the binding pose for ligand molecules independent of the receptor proteins, the semantics-controlled generation of ligands could still further benefit from jointly modeling both the molecular ligand and the receptor protein given sufficient data. Our framework could also be potentially incorporated into diffusion models for pocket-aware ligand design [34, 59], by manipulating the ligand within the confinement of the pocket structure.

In summary, we present a comprehensive exploration of controlled generation of 3D molecules using diffusion models. The design of our framework encourages several desirable behaviors for molecule design, such as precise control over the generative process, disentanglement of the semantic space and flexibility in adapting to diverse tasks requiring control of molecular properties. We demonstrate superior performance in the more challenging tasks with multiple properties and limited data compared to existing baselines, which highlights its potential in extending to real-world applications. We believe that our model, supported by rigorous evaluation and reproducibility, provides a solid foundation for future experimental studies, and offers new hypotheses for further investigation. The initial results of our approach are promising and may inform and guide subsequent validation efforts.

Pre-training dataset: For the pre-training of the MolDiffdAE model, we use the drug-like molecules from GEOM [44] with the same training/validation/test split as previous works [25] as the pre-training dataset.

Fine-tuning dataset (RDKit property): We also build a property dataset for the fine-tuning of MolDiffdAE and training of the property classifiers. Given the semantic embedding z of a known molecule x = (r ,h ,E ) from the encoder, we combine it with randomly sampled stochastic noise x′ = (r′ ,h′ ,E′ ) to generate new molecules x′ = (r′,h′,E′).

Evaluation of generated molecules
Validity, similarity and novelty
To evaluate the quality of generated molecules, we use the following metrics:

• Validity Valid molecules are defined as those that have no violation of valency or disconnected atoms. In practice, this is evaluated by whether the molecule could be successfully processed by RDKit’s SanitizeMol and Kekulize functions.

• Novelty We compare the SMILES of the generated molecules to the training set and report molecules with no overlap as novel. In our experiments, almost all generated molecules are novel.

• Similarity We use RDKit’s TanimotoSimilarity function with default parameters and RDKFingerprint to calculate the 2D Tanimoto similarity, and the ShapeTanimotoDist function to calculate the 3D Tanimoto similarity (ShapeTanimotoSimilarity = 1−ShapeTanimotoDist). In addition, for 3D similarity, the molecules are aligned using GetCrippenO3A from the rdMolAlign module.

Molecular property
The property values of the generated molecules are calculated with RDKit [50] and the TDC [58] oracle, respectively, in the same manner as the fine-tuning dataset.

To evaluate whether the “irrelevant” properties are modified during the manipulation, we select a list of 2D compositional and 3D shape properties that do not overlap with the target properties (all properties in Table S1 excluding fr halogen). For all generated samples, we calculate the mean absolute error (MAE) of the selected irrelevant properties, normalized by the standard deviation of each property.

The contributions of atoms and fragments to properties like LogP and SAS are retrieved from the source code. Specifically, for the labeling in Fig. 4, “high accessibility” fragments are those whose raw contribution score is >2 while “low accessibility” <−0.5. It’s worth noting that RDKit’s SAS output inverts the sum of the contribution scores, so higher contribution leads to lower SAS (i.e., higher synthetic accessibility). For LogP, the labels are based on the scoring table in [53], where negative scores make the molecule more soluble.

Docking
For the CrossDocked test samples, the generated molecules are docked to the respective receptor using QuickVina (version 1.2.5) [56, 57]. Specifically, the coordinates of the generated molecules are shifted to the center point of the source molecule in the original docking conformation. The density function of docking scores is estimated using Gaussian kernel density estimation [70].

Dear editor and reviewers,
We appreciate your efforts in reviewing our submission and your valuable suggestions. In

General response:
We would like to emphasize that unlike many of the diffusion models for 3D molecules
limited to random molecular generation, or a specialized task such as conditional
generation or conformer generation, our model provides a generalizable framework that
could be adapted to many tasks that require finer controls on the generative process. We
experiment with benchmark tasks and also more challenging tasks that require multiple
property manipulation and external datasets with limited labels. Our results show that our
model could successfully control hundreds of molecular properties and manipulate up to
three complex molecular properties. We have verified that the molecules generated for
those more complicated design tasks have comparable and often superior quality with
simpler generative tasks (in terms of the distribution of geometric properties and energy).
This highlights the effectiveness of the semantic guidance, which allows for challenging
design tasks without sacrificing generation quality.
Benchmark and baseline selection
While benchmark datasets like MOSES and GuacaMol have been staples for multiple de
novo drug design tasks, they are not suitable for our 3D-based model because they are 2D
datasets with no structural information, and conformer prediction methods are less
reliable for larger molecules. As our model is specialized for the more challenging and
high-dimensional task of generation of 3D molecules with both 2D and 3D control, we
believe those datasets would not offer much additional insights. Instead, we utilize widely
used benchmark datasets that contain accurate structural information, namely GEOM and
CrossDocked, which provide sufficient information for accurate joint 2D-3D modeling of
drug-like molecules.
Since the property manipulation and controlled generation in equivariant diffusion models
is a less explored problem, we select the baselines and experiments carefully:
1. We included a 2D VAE baseline re-trained on the same training set to demonstrate
the ability of autoencoding equivariant diffusion models to preserve and control the
3D shape
2. We also implemented classifier guidance, a traditional controlled generation
method for diffusion models. Despite its effectiveness in simpler manipulation
tasks, it fails in more complicated tasks, such as multiple properties. Our method,
however, features a disentangled latent space, which enables data-efficient fine-
tuning and manipulation of complex and potentially contradicting properties
3. Furthermore, we did additional experiments and case studies to demonstrate the
importance of controlling 3D geometry, such as loosely preserving the ligand
binding pose
Definition of “disentanglement” and data efficiency
Specifically, we observe that our model is able to identify “disentangled”, Pareto-efficient
directions when manipulating multiple non-orthogonal target properties that could
potentially conflict with each other, while traditional methods such as classifier guidance
would take directions that improve one objective and distract from another. This allows our
model to navigate the high-dimensional, complex molecular and property space with
multiple constraints, and would be particularly helpful for challenging design tasks.
Our proposed method for multiple property manipulation is highly data efficient. We use
small datasets (10% of the training set for RDKit descriptors, 1000 positives for DRD2),
resembling real world scenarios, and simple constrained quadratic optimization and
classifier back-propagation. Despite that, we still outperform traditional methods such as
conditioned diffusion models and classifier guidance, which require large amounts of
labeled data. We believe that more effective and specialized latent space optimization
methods could further enhance the results.
Additional Experiments
To further prove the effectiveness of our method, we have added some additional
experiments:
2.2.1: Interpretation of the latent space through direct molecular retrieval via the semantic
embedding
2.4.3: Enhancing the generation quality of the property manipulation tasks through retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG). We add the results to Fig. 4 and provide a detailed case study
in 2.4.3 and Fig. 8. These experiments demonstrate that:
1. Our latent semantic space is well-regulated and information-rich, and allows direct
retrieval through simple embedding comparison
2. With RAG, even with a simple embedding fusion technique (linear interpolation), we
could further ensure that the manipulated molecules fall within the viable 3D
molecule space
It is also noteworthy that our method is not limited to one diffusion model framework but
could be potentially adapted to other models. Thus, it could benefit from the development
of diffusion models, combining both their generative capacity and our effective semantic
control over the direction of generation. It also has the potential to be easily specialized for
more challenging and customized tasks (such as directly conditioning on protein pocket
structures), as we’ve shown with fine-tuning on external datasets and retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG). We would like to leave them for further studies.
Other important additions include:
Fig 4B: quantitative analysis of the preservation of “irrelevant” properties, further
demonstrating the effectiveness of disentanglement
Supplementary 2.3: energy analysis of generated molecules. We show our model achieves
comparable and often superior molecular energy than the baselines. This shows our model
does not compromise the generation quality despite more challenging generative tasks
and higher model capacity.
Supplementary 2.5: conformer generation by only updating the 3D coordinates. We show
the semantics control slightly improves the validity of generation

analyses of the real experimental results, including raw success counts and individual

molecule). To provide a theoretical insight into the reason behind the success, our
manipulation method looks for a direction in the latent space that points towards higher

## Paper

## Abstract

Controlled generation of 3D molecules is highly valuable in drug design, enabling targeted modifications that preserve core structure and binding-relevant geometry while improving developability-related properties. While equivariant diffusion models achieve state-of-the-art de novo 3D molecule generation, reliably controlling multiple molecular properties remains challenging. A key limitation is structural: A diffusion models typically lack an explicit latent space for targeted manipulation. We propose a semantics-guided equivariant autoencoding diffusion model that learns a disentangled semantic embedding of 3D molecules via an auxiliary encoder, to achieve fine-grained control over the generative denoising process. This semantic embedding enables efficient retrieval, random generation and controlled generation. By directly manipulating the embedding, we effectively steer the molecular generation toward desired compositions, shapes and physicochemical properties, and further enhance the generation quality with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) using the embedding as the query. Importantly, the disentangled embedding offers significant advantages for joint manipulation of multiple properties. Experiments demonstrate precise and data-efficient property control while preserving non-targeted properties.

---

## Introduction

Computational design of molecules has many applications in drug design [1, 2] and protein engineering [3–5]. The 3D geometry of molecules holds significant implications for their properties and functions, such as quantum chemical properties [6, 7], molecular dynamics [8–10], and interactions with protein receptors [11, 12]. Recently, generative modeling of 3D molecules has been an active area of research. To properly represent the 3D geometry, some methods learn a joint distribution over the geometric features [4, 13]. Others directly operate on the 3D molecular space [14]. Specifically, equivariant diffusion models have achieved state-of-the-art results in generating high-quality 3D molecules [15–17], and also in design tasks with external conditioning, such as ligands conditioned on protein receptors [18, 19] and linkers conditioned on molecular fragments [20]. Diffusion models belong to the class of generative models designed to approximate the data distribution by iterative denoising from corrupted data [21, 22]. Unlike previous methods for molecule generation that rely on autoregressive generation, diffusion models perform simultaneous refinement of all elements, such as atoms, charges and bonds, in each denoising iteration. This collective refinement approach enables them to effectively capture the underlying data structures, making them well-suited for structured generation such as 3D molecules. Several recent studies further incorporate auxiliary information, such as bond connectivity, to improve the generation quality [23–25].

However, the majority of these works focus on de novo generation, i.e., generating random 3D molecules with no or limited control over their compositions, structures and properties, which we collectively define in this work as “semantics”. In real-world applications such as drug design, it would be desirable to ensure that the generated molecules contain certain attributes through explicit control of the generation process. Some previous works focus on the controlled generation of 2D graphs [1, 26–32], while controlling 3D molecule generation remains a challenge due to the complexity of the 3D molecular space and the need to preserve the 3D geometry. Some recent studies achieve conditioning on selected molecular properties [15, 33, 34] or 3D shapes [35]. These methods, despite being effective on the designated tasks, only control a narrow portion of the generation process, and cannot be easily generalized to multiple or novel conditions without training a new conditional generative model. On the other hand, it is uncertain how conditioning affects the interactions among properties due to their complex interplay, and manually disentangling them is non-trivial and time-consuming. For example, a lead compound may require higher water solubility and easier synthesis. Meanwhile, the backbone composition, the 3D shape and subsequently the protein binding affinity of the lead compound should also be preserved. As these objectives do not necessarily align, the generation process that fulfills one objective may potentially interfere with another, and naively conditioning on multiple objectives without proper regularization may fail to find a direction that satisfies all. To overcome these limitations, it is thus essential to implement a refined control mechanism that both captures the comprehensive context of molecular compositions and shapes, and automatically disentangles the intricate interdependencies between the properties.

Controlled generation with diffusion models in particular poses another challenge as these models lack an explicit latent space to operate on. The latent diffusion model [36] is trained on the low-dimensional latent space of another generative model, but the diffusion model’s own latent space is still implicit and difficult to control. Thus, controlled generation is usually achieved by external guidance on the denoising process. For example, classifier guidance [37] and classifier-free guidance [38] can generate random samples conditioned on certain properties. These methods have high demands on the availability of labeled data, and generalize poorly to new or multiple objectives. Some studies utilize external, pre-trained molecular representations as conditions [39]. Though such representations could be highly informative, there is no theoretical guarantee of the effectiveness of their control, and they cannot be easily manipulated. Thus, for data-efficient control of multiple molecular properties, we could leverage an unsupervised latent space that captures the complete semantic information about molecular structures and compositions and use it to guide the generation process of diffusion models.

In this work, we propose MolDiffdAE, a disentangled autoencoding equivariant diffusion model controlled by an unsupervised, higher-level semantic embedding of the molecule, inspired by the idea of semantic guidance of diffusion models for controlled generation of images [40–42]. The semantic embedding is co-trained with the diffusion model and is set up to have three important features that address the aforementioned challenges: (1) maximal mutual information with the input that guarantees complete semantic information about the molecule; (2) strong and precise control over the generation process of the diffusion model that effectively translates the semantics into the 3D molecular space; (3) disentangled semantic space through distributional regularization, which empirically enables conditioning on multiple properties with minimal internal interference, yielding Pareto-efficient control directions. By directly operating on the semantic embedding, we could control and manipulate the compositional and structural features of the generated molecules, as well as higher-level properties. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in two types of generative tasks: (1) semantics-guided generation, where we use predefined semantics to generate random molecules that contain the desired semantic information; (2) property manipulation, where certain properties of known source molecules are modified through altering the respective dimensions of the semantic embedding. We then evaluate whether the generated molecules exhibit the specified property(ies). We summarize our main contributions as follows:

• We perform a comprehensive analysis of controlled 3D molecule generation and manipulation using diffusion models. We also establish the benchmark tasks and evaluation metrics for the subject. We prove that the semantic embedding learned by our model has a theoretical guarantee of maximal mutual information with the molecule, and demonstrate effective control over more than 200 molecular properties.

• We transform the challenging task of controlled molecule generation using 3D equivariant diffusion models, often requiring sufficient labeled data or accurate classifiers, to the more data-efficient task of latent space optimization (LSO). Thus, our model could be flexibly applied to challenging molecular design tasks where labeled data is scarce and complex relations are present among the objectives. We show that the semantic embedding also allows fast querying of the molecular space and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to further enhance the generation quality.

• Compared to existing baseline methods, we report the highest performance on multi-objective property manipulation, a task hindered by the difficulty of regularizing the latent space of diffusion models, which we mitigate through the disentanglement constraints on the semantic space.

---

## Results

Semantics-guided diffusion generation framework
Our proposed MolDiffdAE model is an autoencoding framework that utilizes a semantic embedding to control the generation of the equivariant diffusion model. The model has two important features:

• The semantic embedding has maximal mutual information with the input molecule and comprehensively controls all aspects of the generation.

• The disentanglement of the semantic embedding space facilitates the manipulation of multiple objectives, encouraging the model to find directions that achieve all objectives with minimal conflicts.

We implement an encoder that learns the higher-level “semantics” of the input 3D molecule as a continuous, lower-dimensional vector z, aggregating both node- and edge-wise features. The semantic embedding is then provided to an equivariant diffusion model as a condition. The diffusion model functions as a “decoder” that translates the semantic embedding back to the 3D molecular space. (Fig. 1A). During training, the model attempts to predict the clean input data from corrupted data and the semantic embedding. We apply a Wasserstein loss [43] that minimizes the distance between the distribution of the semantic latent space and a prior distribution p(z). In our case, p(z) is an isotropic Gaussian distribution N(0,I). We show that this regularization ensures maximal mutual information between the embedding and the input, and also achieves disentanglement between the dimensions. This leads to our objective function:
L = L (θ) + βL , (1)
dAE D Wass
where L (θ) is the diffusion loss (Eq. 8), L is the Wasserstein loss and β > 0 is the regularization coefficient. The semantic encoder and the diffusion decoder are trained simultaneously on unlabeled 3D molecule conformations from the GEOM dataset [44] in an unsupervised manner. We term this as the pre-trained model.

For the downstream tasks, we could further perform supervised fine-tuning on molecular properties. Specifically, we add an auxiliary classifier on top of the semantic embedding to predict the target property, then train the classifier, encoder and diffusion model in an end-to-end manner with an additional classifier loss:
L = L (θ) + βL + β′L .
dAE-ft D Wass cls
In this work, we only fine-tune on three more complex properties, QED (drug-likeness), SAS (synthetic accessibility) and LogP (lipophilicity, inversely related to water solubility), as we find their prediction with the pre-trained embedding more difficult (Fig. S2). These properties involve intricate interactions between the structural patterns distributed across the atoms, and cannot be learned without supervision, necessitating the fine-tuning. Since property calculation is time-consuming and reliable labeled data is usually rare in real-world scenarios, we construct a fine-tuning dataset by sub-sampling 10% of the pre-training dataset. We denote the pre-trained model as MolDiffdAE and the fine-tuned model as MolDiffdAE-ft.

We then use the diffusion decoder to flexibly perform controlled generation with the semantic embeddings (Fig. 1B, C). As shown in Methods, the embedding z shares maximal mutual information with the input x . Thus, the generated molecule will presumably possess the properties encoded by the embedding. It is also possible to alter certain properties of interest by directly manipulating the embedding. In this way, we transform the challenging problem of controlled generation with diffusion models into a task of latent space optimization (LSO), where several methods could be applied to obtain the desired semantic embedding, which is then translated into the 3D molecular space.

A detailed comparison between molecular generation frameworks can be found in Table 1. Our proposed model combines the high 3D molecular generation capacity of the 3D diffusion model, and the controllability of autoencoding models. In addition, the disentangled semantic space also enables flexible multi-objective manipulation, which is difficult for conditioned generative models that require abundant labeled data and re-training for each objective. These features extend the model capacity beyond less controlled generative tasks such as de novo design and conditioning on single objectives.

Semantics-based molecular retrieval
To interpret the latent semantic space, we perform molecular retrieval from the training set with a query embedding vector z. We use z of existing molecules in the test set as queries. Specifically, we calculate the cosine similarity between each query (source) molecule embedding z and the embedding z* of each molecule in the training set, and then retrieve molecules with the highest cosine similarity to the source.

Shown in Fig. 2A, molecules retrieved by the same query embedding display similar compositions to the source molecule. Quantitatively, the retrieved molecules show significantly higher 2D and 3D Tanimoto similarity to the source molecule, as compared to random pairings (Fig. 2B). In conclusion, we could efficiently query the molecular space and retrieve molecules with desired composition, shape and properties, indicating a semantics-rich latent space that could be used for controlled generation and manipulation.

Probing the property information in the latent semantic space
We train linear regression models to predict the molecular properties from the embeddings, to probe the information content of the semantic space. Despite being trained in an unsupervised manner unaware of any property label, the embedding space of the pre-trained MolDiffdAE could accurately predict many of the properties (Fig. S2A). The dimensions of the embedding can be distinguishably clustered by their differential linear regression coefficients with respect to the properties (Fig. S3). Specifically, only a limited, distinct set of dimensions significantly contribute to each property (Fig. 2C). Also, the embedding space shows strong separation of the high- and low-value groups for many of the properties (Fig. 2E). More complex properties like QED, SAS and LogP are harder to capture with the pre-training. Nevertheless, MolDiffdAE-ft fine-tuned on those properties shows higher predictive performance (Fig. S2B), sparser and more divergent contributions (Fig. 2D), and a better-separated latent space (Fig. 2F), while the fine-tuning has negligible impact on the other properties. Quantitative analysis also shows better disentanglement of the latent space after fine-tuning (Table S2). Meanwhile, the embedding dimensions have minimal internal correlations (Fig. S6A). These results indicate the successful disentanglement between the dimensions enforced by the Wasserstein loss.

Semantics-guided 3D molecule generation
To evaluate the effectiveness of the semantic control over the generation process of the equivariant diffusion model, we explore ways of utilizing it for the generation of 3D molecules with complete semantic information. Specifically, we investigate whether all the molecular properties encoded by the semantics could be successfully translated into the generated molecule.

We obtain the semantic embedding z of known source molecules x from the encoder and perform controlled generation using both deterministic (denoising diffusion implicit model; DDIM [22]) and stochastic (denoising diffusion probabilistic model; DDPM [21]) methods. For DDPM, we generate 10 molecules from each embedding and report metrics on valid molecules only. Fig. S4A shows that DDIM with MolDiffdAE gives near-perfect reconstruction as expected, while DDPM generates molecules that are very close to the source molecule in terms of both composition and 3D shape. This shows that the embedding z dominates the denoising process, while the stochasticity accounts for minor variations.

For a quantitative evaluation of the preservation of the semantics, we define a molecular property profile including 205 non-zero-variance properties calculated by RDKit [50]. We report the following metrics between the generated molecules from DDPM and the source: (1) mean absolute error (MAE) of the properties, aggregated from the selected 2D and 3D property groups (see Table S1 for the full list); (2) Tanimoto similarity (|F ∩F |/|F ∪F | where F ,F are two feature sets) of 2D and 3D fingerprints. We benchmark against the following methods:

• VAE (2D): We use a 2D graph-based variational autoencoder (VAE) to generate random molecules from the embeddings of the source molecules. The generated molecules are represented as SMILES [51] sequences. The 3D properties and 3D Tanimoto similarity of the generated molecules are calculated based on the RDKit-predicted conformations.

• Classifier Guidance: We train a basic equivariant diffusion model without supervision and an independent classifier that predicts all 205 properties. We then use the gradient of the classifier to guide the generation process of a basic diffusion model toward the property profile of the source molecule.

• Random: We use the following methods to obtain the background distribution of the metrics: (1) Property MAE: we randomly sample property values from a N(µ ,σ ) distribution where µ ,σ are the mean and standard deviation of the property, then compare them with those of the source; (2) Tanimoto similarity: for each source molecule, we randomly sample 10 molecules from the training set then calculate their 2D and 3D Tanimoto similarity with the source.

Table 2 shows the aggregated MAEs, along with a detailed breakdown of example individual properties, and average Tanimoto similarities. As expected, the 2D graph-based VAE achieves good preservation of 2D properties, but not of 3D properties. For the 3D structure-based models, MolDiffdAE achieves better preservation of most of the properties than classifier guidance, including both 2D compositional and 3D geometric features. The generated molecules are also more similar to their sources. Notably, unlike classifier guidance where a separate classifier is trained on an external labeled dataset, MolDiffdAE is pre-trained in an unsupervised manner completely unaware of any property. We observe similar performance on randomly sampled semantic embeddings from N(0,I) (Fig. S4B; Supplementary).

These results show that the unsupervised embedding successfully captures the semantic information about the 3D molecular properties and translates it into the generated molecules, indicating effective control over the generation of the equivariant diffusion model. Consequently, leveraging molecular generation based on the semantic embedding of known molecules facilitates the exploration of their neighborhoods in the molecular space in terms of compositions, structures, and properties.

In addition to the generation of full molecules, our model can also adapt to the problem of conformer generation, by fixing the atom and bond types during the denoising process (Supplementary). Despite not being trained specifically on this task, our model shows superior performance to similar models and baselines (Table S5), demonstrating the effectiveness of the semantic control.

Multi-objective molecular property manipulation
In this section, we further explore a generative task that requires more precise control: using the semantic embedding to manipulate the properties of interest, while preserving the majority of composition features, 3D shape and unrelated properties as much as possible. The problem is formulated as follows: let z be the embedding of a molecule x and y = (y ,...,y ) be its property value(s) (p ∈P ,P ⊆P where P is the complete property set and P is the set of properties of interest). Given the desired target property value(s) y′ = (y′ ,...,y′ ), we search the latent space for a new embedding z′ that maps to a new molecule x′ which exhibits the target property y′, while remaining sufficiently similar to x. The latter can be achieved by minimizing the deviation of z′ from z.

We experiment with two ways of obtaining z′:

• Linear manipulation (lm): We first train a linear regression model y = Wz+b (z ∈ R1×d; y ,b ∈ R1×m; W ∈ Rm×d; d is the dimension of z and m is the number of properties) to predict the properties from the embedding, then use it to manipulate the source embedding via:
z′ ← z + W+(y′ − b − Wz) (2)
where W+ ∈ Rd×m is the pseudo-inverse of W, i.e., WW+W = W. It can be proved that z′ is the closest vector to z (in terms of ||z′ − z|| ) that predicts the target property y′ (see Methods and Supplementary for more details).

• Classifier back-propagation (bp): We take the auxiliary classifier of the fine-tuned model and iteratively back-propagate the gradient of the classification loss L to z (Algorithm 1). This is only performed on the fine-tuned properties (QED, SAS, LogP).

On top of direct manipulation, we also experiment with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [52] for the fine-tuned properties (QED, SAS, LogP). Specifically, we use the manipulated embedding z′ from classifier back-propagation (bp) to retrieve the 10 closest embeddings from the training set by cosine similarity. The retrieved embeddings (z*) are used to enhance the generation quality via two methods:

• Interpolation (RAG-interp): The retrieved embedding z* is fused with the manipulated embedding z′ through simple interpolation: z′ ← (1−λ)z′ + λz*. We use λ=0.25.

• Second-round manipulation (RAG-reopt): We further manipulate the interpolated embedding toward the same target using classifier back-propagation (bp).

Specifically, we use the deterministic DDIM generation process because it offers stronger control than stochastic DDPM. We first deterministically reverse the diffusion model to map the source molecule x to a noise point x , then perform denoising from x conditioned on the manipulated embedding z′.

We compare our method with the following baselines (see Methods for more details; all diffusion model-based methods start from the deterministically reverse-mapped noise x ):

• VAE (2D)+lm: We perform the same linear manipulation method as MolDiffdAE+lm on the embeddings of the 2D graph VAE. Similar to DDIM, the decoding is also deterministic, as no noise is added to the embedding.

• Conditioned Diffusion: We train a diffusion model conditioned on the property subset P and use it to generate the manipulated molecule conditioned on the target property value y′.

• Classifier Guidance: We train an independent classifier for each property and use it to perform classifier guidance on the basic equivariant diffusion model toward the target property value y′.

• Random Diffusion: We randomly generate molecules with the same atom number as the source using the simple diffusion model with DDPM generation.

• Random MolDiffdAE: We use randomly sampled embeddings from N(0,I) to guide the generation of MolDiffdAE. This reflects the background distribution of the semantic embedding space.

We use a one-pass, deterministic generation method where the encoder and decoder are each called only once per sample. Ideally, the minimal alteration to the semantic embedding during the manipulation implicitly preserves the similarity with the source, and no explicit similarity constraint is needed. For a fair comparison, the same generation mode is also applied to all baselines (see Methods for more details).

On simpler tasks with single properties, our model shows competitive performance with classifier guidance (Fig. S12). We then evaluate our model on more challenging tasks where multiple properties are manipulated simultaneously.

Overall performance on multi-objective manipulation tasks
For the multi-objective tasks, we jointly manipulate 2 or 3 properties selected from halogen count (fr halogen), QED, SAS and LogP. Specifically, we set our objective as lower SAS for easier synthesis, lower LogP for higher water solubility, higher QED for higher drug-likeness, and either higher or lower number of halogens. We define “improvement” for each objective as the change of the value of the property p ∈P adjusted by the desired manipulation direction:
∆ = (yˆ′ − y(0) for increasing objectives (“+”)
pi pi
(y(0) − yˆ′ for decreasing objectives (“–”),
pi pi
where yˆ′ is the property value achieved by the manipulated molecule and y(0) is that of the source molecule. By this definition, more positive improvement is always preferred regardless of the manipulation direction.

We report “success” cases where (1) the generated molecule is valid and novel (not observed in the training set; Fig. S8); (2) the 3D Tanimoto similarity between the generated molecule and the source is greater than 0.5 (95% quantile of random pairwise similarity; Fig. S7); (3) all properties have improvements above a given threshold, where σ is the standard deviation of the property p . We use either a relaxed (>0) or strict (>0.5σ ) improvement threshold. Fig. 3A demonstrates that MolDiffdAE-based methods perform significantly better than the baselines in all but one task, especially under strict improvement thresholds. Furthermore, fine-tuning, back-propagation manipulation and RAG, when applicable, could enhance the overall performance, especially on the more complex properties (QED, SAS, LogP). Meanwhile, the majority of the compositional and structural patterns are well preserved as the manipulated molecules remain similar to their sources qualitatively (Fig. 3C,D,E, I; Fig. S10A). We also show that our methods achieve better numerical preservation of the irrelevant molecular properties, especially with fine-tuning and RAG (Fig. 3B; see Methods for more details).

A detailed analysis of the improvements shows that MolDiffdAE-manipulated molecules generally achieve a better trade-off between all objectives, while classifier guidance occasionally succeeds in one objective but fails in the others (Fig. 3D, F, H; Fig. S10B). These results highlight the advantage of MolDiffdAE’s well-regularized and disentangled latent space, as the objectives have minimal interference with each other. We also observe that the 2D graph-based VAE achieves reasonable success in manipulating the target properties (Table S7), but fails to preserve the 3D similarity, leading to lower final performance. MolDiffdAE, on the other hand, could better preserve both the composition and shape due to the strong semantic control.

In addition, we also analyze the geometric features (Table S4) and conformer energy (Fig. S5A) of the generated molecules, where MolDiffdAE-based methods, especially when combined with classifier back-propagation and RAG, display higher generation quality, indicating a well-regularized latent semantic space that facilitates smooth exploration. In the following sections, we provide a more comprehensive and in-depth analysis of MolDiffdAE’s controlled generation capacity, by investigating its manipulation behavior regarding molecular fragments, preservation of 3D shapes and protein interactions, and ability to manipulate 3D properties.

Case study 1: Joint manipulation of LogP and SAS
We perform an in-depth comparison between the manipulation results targeting both lower LogP (higher water solubility) and lower SAS (higher synthetic accessibility) for MolDiffdAE-based manipulation and classifier guidance. These properties are ideal targets for evaluating the impact of the disentangled latent space, as both of them are defined by the combined contribution of the molecular fragments: LogP is calculated as the sum of the hydrophilicity score of each atom [53], and SAS based on the frequencies of the fragments, as more common fragments imply easier synthesis [54]. As a result, different fragments may have aligned or diverging impacts on LogP and SAS. Thus, it is important for the property manipulation process to separate their differential contributions, and introduce fragments that contribute to both objectives.

In the first example (Fig. 4A), classifier guidance successfully reduces the SAS score by replacing the low accessibility backbone with a high accessibility one. However, some of these newly introduced fragments also reduce water solubility. For example, additional benzene rings are highly accessible but less water-soluble. Similarly, in Fig. 4B, the low accessibility backbone is modified, but solubility is not improved as the new backbone does not include more hydrophilic atoms. In comparison, manipulation with MolDiffdAE successfully considers both objectives, as it introduces fragments that are both more synthetically accessible and more water-soluble.

We further complicate the task by adding “more halogens” as another objective. This objective could interfere with the reduction of LogP as halogens are hydrophobic. Meanwhile, aromatic carbons bound to halogens would slightly increase water solubility as a result of the polarization of the aromatic ring. We show that on top of the aforementioned behaviors, MolDiffdAE-based manipulation also tends to attach halogens to aromatic rings to counteract the hydrophobic effect of halogens, while avoiding aliphatic carbons (Fig. 4C, D). In contrast, classifier guidance could trivially succeed in increasing the number of halogens, but fail to make other necessary modifications accordingly to reduce LogP (Fig. 4C) or SAS (Fig. 4D).

These results further prove that the disentangled semantic space successfully guides the diffusion model in multi-objective manipulation tasks. Manipulation in the disentangled semantic embedding space of MolDiffdAE could identify directions that simultaneously satisfy all objectives. With simple classifier guidance, however, the gradient of the classifiers could lead to conflicting directions and interfere with each other without proper regularization.

Case study 2: Validity enhancement by retrieval-augmented generation
We observe that using RAG achieves competitive results with MolDiffdAE-ft+bp, the best-performing method without RAG, in the tasks involving QED, SAS and LogP, and noticeably better results under relaxed improvement thresholds (> 0). A detailed analysis shows comparable performance in terms of success rate (Fig. 3A) and similarity to the source (Fig. 5A, top) between the MolDiffdAE-based methods, while RAG noticeably improves the validity of the generated molecules (Fig. 5A, middle). We also show that the generation quality is overall higher with RAG, in terms of the distribution of geometric properties (Fig. 5A, bottom; Table S4). We notice no significant performance differences between the two RAG methods tested.

Fig. 5B shows that in some of the success cases, the retrieved molecules already contain the desired target properties, due to an information-rich and structured latent space. More importantly, the generated molecule incorporates compositional features from both the source molecule and the retrieved molecule, potentially enhancing the generation quality by keeping the manipulated embedding closer to the data distribution.

External Application 1: Binding-preserving property manipulation
Due to its ability to preserve 3D shapes, which is closely related to the interaction conformations, our semantics-guided property manipulation is particularly useful for protein-binding ligands. In those cases, the binding toward the target protein should be maintained, while some useful properties such as QED, LogP and SAS are modified. To test the generalizability of our method to this task, we apply both our pre-trained and fine-tuned model to the external test set of CrossDocked [55], which contains the 3D structure of 100 ligand-receptor pairs. We observe that MolDiffdAE-based methods show competitive performance with classifier guidance on single-objective tasks (Table S6), and significantly higher performance on multi-objective tasks (Fig. 6A).

We then dock the manipulated molecules back to their respective receptors using QuickVina [56, 57]. Fig. 6B shows examples where the docking is mostly maintained after manipulating the target properties, as reflected by similar docking scores. Overall, on top of successes in improving the target properties, MolDiffdAE-based manipulation could also preserve the Vina score distribution of the source molecules. Meanwhile, classifier guidance preserves the 3D shape and docking but fails in the manipulation objective (Fig. 6A), while 2D VAE-based manipulation breaks the docking (Fig. 6C, D). These results are particularly compelling as our MolDiffdAE model is not explicitly conditioned on the structure of the receptor, but could still maintain the binding throughout the property manipulation. Thus, it could be used to manipulate lead compounds without the need to jointly model both the ligand and the receptor, as the preservation of the 3D shape implicitly preserves the docking. As reliable structures for ligand-receptor complexes are relatively rare, our method could efficiently transfer the 3D shape knowledge from the more data-rich domain of isolated 3D molecules to the generation and manipulation of ligands. It is noteworthy that the method only preserves the 3D shape not necessarily the binding itself, which would require fine-tuning with the protein pocket as the direct conditioning. We leave these for further studies.

External Application 2: Manipulation of DRD2 binding affinity
Beyond basic molecular properties, we further test our method on more complex external properties. We focus on increasing the binding affinity to the dopamine D2 receptor (DRD2). Despite being a well-studied benchmark, the 3D structural data for positive DRD2 binders is still relatively scarce. We select 1400 positive structures from GEOM using the oracle predictor provided by the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) [58]. Due to the complex nature of protein binding, the small data size makes it difficult to train reliable 3D structure-based classifiers or conditioned diffusion models. We fine-tune our MolDiffdAE model on the DRD2 binding dataset, achieving good separation of positives and negatives in the semantic space (Fig. 7A), and perform linear manipulation to increase the binding affinity score. The generated molecules are then evaluated by the same oracle model, and we report positive molecules with binding score >0.5.

As shown in Fig. 7B, MolDiffdAE-ft with linear manipulation outperforms all baselines with a simple one-pass generation and no post-generation filtering. This implies that fine-tuning of the latent semantic space enables efficient use of the limited labeled data. We observe that the manipulated molecules have more hydrophobic components, such as aliphatic carbon (Fig. 7C), naturally resulting in higher LogP (Fig. 7D, bottom). This encourages binding toward DRD2’s highly hydrophobic pocket. Also, though not an explicit objective, the manipulated molecules also show higher QED (Fig. 7D, top), indicating underlying mutual factors that contribute to both DRD2 binding and drug-likeness. However, the manipulation also increases synthetic difficulty (higher SAS; Fig. 7D, middle). This could be potentially improved by jointly manipulating SAS as well, as in previous experiments.

Manipulation of 3D properties
Most of the existing works for controlled molecular generation are restricted to compositional properties, due to their limitations of relying on sequence or 2D graph representations, while the manipulation of 3D geometric properties remains poorly explored. MolDiffdAE as an equivariant 3D diffusion model enables operation on those properties. We manipulate asphericity (Asp) and radius of gyration (RoG) with linear manipulation. As expected, the 2D VAE fails in controlling the 3D properties. Among the 3D equivariant model-based methods, MolDiffdAE shows superior performance in both single- and multi-objective tasks, especially under more stringent improvement thresholds (>0.5σ ) (Fig. 8A).

Contrary to our previous results on compositional properties where the composition undergoes drastic changes while the 3D shape is mostly preserved, manipulation of the 3D properties typically leads to major alterations in the 3D shapes compared to the source molecules (Fig. 8B). In agreement with common observations, molecules with higher asphericity are less spherical, while molecules with higher radius of gyration are more spatially stretched. Meanwhile, the composition of the source is well-preserved after the manipulation. We also observe a good trade-off between the objectives with MolDiffdAE, while classifier guidance either fails in achieving both objectives, or generates few valid molecules (Fig. 8C). The latter suggests the complexity of 3D geometries and implies the usefulness of encoding the 3D structural information into the molecular semantics. Such tasks would be useful in the search of candidate molecules with a preferred 3D shape and a fixed chemical composition.

Discussion
In this study, we present MolDiffdAE, an equivariant diffusion model guided by a disentangled semantic latent space for the controlled generation of 3D molecules. We show that the semantic embedding effectively controls the composition, shape, and molecular properties of the generated molecules, in both stochastic generation and deterministic property manipulation. More importantly, the regularization-induced disentanglement of the semantic embedding empowers effective multi-objective manipulation, which is a challenge for traditional diffusion models where the latent space is entangled and difficult to operate on. Though trained in an unsupervised manner, our pre-trained model is capable of capturing simple compositional and 3D shape properties, and can be used to manipulate them through the semantic embedding. For more complex properties whose contributing factors are distributed across many atoms, such as drug-likeness, solubility, synthetic accessibility and protein binding affinity, we show that our model could be further fine-tuned on small, external property-labeled datasets to enhance the performance.

Several existing controlled molecule generation frameworks on 2D molecules deploy iterative optimization or post-generation filtering to ensure the generation quality and the similarity to the source molecule if required [1, 29]. Our method, however, uses one-pass generation, calling the diffusion decoder only once, and evaluating only the final generation output. Similarity constraint is implicitly enforced by minimizing the distance to the source semantic embedding. Despite the simplified generation pipeline, our method already achieves a good success rate with respect to molecular validity, property values and similarity to the source, as a result of the strong guidance of the semantic embedding and the high capacity of the diffusion model. We also show that the information-rich, low-dimensional semantic embedding vector can be efficiently used for the retrieval of similar molecules and subsequently the enhancement of manipulation results through RAG. Nevertheless, the generation quality of our model could also be further improved through iterative refinement or encoding of the molecular similarity into the latent semantic space with contrastive learning. It is also worth noting that in our experiments, we use randomly sampled “negative” source molecules, some of which may be too challenging for the target value. In real applications, a rational pre-selection of more promising source molecules could further enhance the success rate.

Beyond basic molecular properties, we expect the method to be applicable to a wide spectrum of objectives, such as toxicity, conformational energy, multi-receptor binding affinity, and material properties. It is also possible to associate the semantic embedding with text descriptions, and utilize the recent advances in large language models (LLM) for more flexible conditioning and control [32]. Our framework could also flexibly incorporate recent advances in representation learning and diffusion model architectures for 3D molecules, to enhance the representativeness of the latent space, the quality of generation, and the generalization to rarer and more complex structures. Specifically, using generative models with greater flexibility could enable more drastic manipulations, which is common in real-world drug design and optimization.

Furthermore, although we have demonstrated the preservation of the 3D shape and the binding pose for ligand molecules independent of the receptor proteins, the semantics-controlled generation of ligands could still further benefit from jointly modeling both the molecular ligand and the receptor protein given sufficient data. Our framework could also be potentially incorporated into diffusion models for pocket-aware ligand design [34, 59], by manipulating the ligand within the confinement of the pocket structure.

In summary, we present a comprehensive exploration of controlled generation of 3D molecules using diffusion models. The design of our framework encourages several desirable behaviors for molecule design, such as precise control over the generative process, disentanglement of the semantic space and flexibility in adapting to diverse tasks requiring control of molecular properties. We demonstrate superior performance in the more challenging tasks with multiple properties and limited data compared to existing baselines, which highlights its potential in extending to real-world applications. We believe that our model, supported by rigorous evaluation and reproducibility, provides a solid foundation for future experimental studies, and offers new hypotheses for further investigation. The initial results of our approach are promising and may inform and guide subsequent validation efforts.

Pre-training dataset: For the pre-training of the MolDiffdAE model, we use the drug-like molecules from GEOM [44] with the same training/validation/test split as previous works [25] as the pre-training dataset.

Fine-tuning dataset (RDKit property): We also build a property dataset for the fine-tuning of MolDiffdAE and training of the property classifiers. Specifically, we use RDKit (version 2024.3.2) to calculate the properties of the samples in the validation set of the pre-training dataset, resulting in a dataset comprising 10% of the pre-training set.

Evaluation of generated molecules
Validity, similarity and novelty
To evaluate the quality of generated molecules, we use the following metrics:

• Validity Valid molecules are defined as those that have no violation of valency or disconnected atoms. In practice, this is evaluated by whether the molecule could be successfully processed by RDKit’s SanitizeMol and Kekulize functions.

• Novelty We compare the SMILES of the generated molecules to the training set and report molecules with no overlap as novel. In our experiments, almost all generated molecules are novel.

• Similarity We use RDKit’s TanimotoSimilarity function with default parameters and RDKFingerprint to calculate the 2D Tanimoto similarity, and the ShapeTanimotoDist function to calculate the 3D Tanimoto similarity (ShapeTanimotoSimilarity = 1−ShapeTanimotoDist). In addition, for 3D similarity, the molecules are aligned using GetCrippenO3A from the rdMolAlign module.

Molecular property
The property values of the generated molecules are calculated with RDKit [50] and the TDC [58] oracle, respectively, in the same manner as the fine-tuning dataset.

To evaluate whether the “irrelevant” properties are modified during the manipulation, we select a list of 2D compositional and 3D shape properties that do not overlap with the target properties (all properties in Table S1 excluding fr halogen). For all generated samples, we calculate the mean absolute error (MAE) of the selected irrelevant properties, normalized by the standard deviation of each property.

The contributions of atoms and fragments to properties like LogP and SAS are retrieved from the source code. Specifically, for the labeling in Fig. 4, “high accessibility” fragments are those whose raw contribution score is >2 while “low accessibility” <−0.5. It’s worth noting that RDKit’s SAS output inverts the sum of the contribution scores, so higher contribution leads to lower SAS (i.e., higher synthetic accessibility). For LogP, the labels are based on the scoring table in [53], where negative scores make the molecule more soluble.

Docking
For the CrossDocked test samples, the generated molecules are docked to the respective receptor using QuickVina (version 1.2.5) [56, 57]. Specifically, the coordinates of the generated molecules are shifted to the center point of the source molecule in the original docking conformation. The density function of docking scores is estimated using Gaussian kernel density estimation [70].

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Dear editor and reviewers,
We appreciate your efforts in reviewing our submission and your valuable suggestions. In
the updated manuscript, we have addressed the reviewers’ comments with updated
experimental results and analysis. Major updates are highlighted.
General response:
We would like to emphasize that unlike many of the diffusion models for 3D molecules
limited to random molecular generation, or a specialized task such as conditional
generation or conformer generation, our model provides a generalizable framework that
could be adapted to many tasks that require finer controls on the generative process. We
experiment with benchmark tasks and also more challenging tasks that require multiple
property manipulation and external datasets with limited labels. Our results show that our
model could successfully control hundreds of molecular properties and manipulate up to
three complex molecular properties. We have verified that the molecules generated for
those more complicated design tasks have comparable and often superior quality with
simpler generative tasks (in terms of the distribution of geometric properties and energy).
This highlights the effectiveness of the semantic guidance, which allows for challenging
design tasks without sacrificing generation quality.
Benchmark and baseline selection
While benchmark datasets like MOSES and GuacaMol have been staples for multiple de
novo drug design tasks, they are not suitable for our 3D-based model because they are 2D
datasets with no structural information, and conformer prediction methods are less
reliable for larger molecules. As our model is specialized for the more challenging and
high-dimensional task of generation of 3D molecules with both 2D and 3D control, we
believe those datasets would not offer much additional insights. Instead, we utilize widely
used benchmark datasets that contain accurate structural information, namely GEOM and
CrossDocked, which provide sufficient information for accurate joint 2D-3D modeling of
drug-like molecules.
Since the property manipulation and controlled generation in equivariant diffusion models
is a less explored problem, we select the baselines and experiments carefully:
1. We included a 2D VAE baseline re-trained on the same training set to demonstrate
the ability of autoencoding equivariant diffusion models to preserve and control the
3D shape
2. We also implemented classifier guidance, a traditional controlled generation
method for diffusion models. Despite its effectiveness in simpler manipulation
tasks, it fails in more complicated tasks, such as multiple properties. Our method,
however, features a disentangled latent space, which enables data-efficient fine-
tuning and manipulation of complex and potentially contradicting properties
3. Furthermore, we did additional experiments and case studies to demonstrate the
importance of controlling 3D geometry, such as loosely preserving the ligand
binding pose
Definition of “disentanglement” and data efficiency
Specifically, we observe that our model is able to identify “disentangled”, Pareto-efficient
directions when manipulating multiple non-orthogonal target properties that could
potentially conflict with each other, while traditional methods such as classifier guidance
would take directions that improve one objective and distract from another. This allows our
model to navigate the high-dimensional, complex molecular and property space with
multiple constraints, and would be particularly helpful for challenging design tasks.
Our proposed method for multiple property manipulation is highly data efficient. We use
small datasets (10% of the training set for RDKit descriptors, 1000 positives for DRD2),
resembling real world scenarios, and simple constrained quadratic optimization and
classifier back-propagation. Despite that, we still outperform traditional methods such as
conditioned diffusion models and classifier guidance, which require large amounts of
labeled data. We believe that more effective and specialized latent space optimization
methods could further enhance the results.
Additional Experiments
To further prove the effectiveness of our method, we have added some additional
experiments:
2.2.1: Interpretation of the latent space through direct molecular retrieval via the semantic
embedding
2.4.3: Enhancing the generation quality of the property manipulation tasks through retrieval-
augmented generation (RAG). We add the results to Fig. 4 and provide a detailed case study
in 2.4.3 and Fig. 8. These experiments demonstrate that:
1. Our latent semantic space is well-regulated and information-rich, and allows direct
retrieval through simple embedding comparison
2. With RAG, even with a simple embedding fusion technique (linear interpolation), we
could further ensure that the manipulated molecules fall within the viable 3D
molecule space
It is also noteworthy that our method is not limited to one diffusion model framework but
could be potentially adapted to other models. Thus, it could benefit from the development
of diffusion models, combining both their generative capacity and our effective semantic
control over the direction of generation. It also has the potential to be easily specialized for
more challenging and customized tasks (such as directly conditioning on protein pocket
structures), as we’ve shown with fine-tuning on external datasets and retrieval-augmented
generation (RAG). We would like to leave them for further studies.
Other important additions include:
Fig 4B: quantitative analysis of the preservation of “irrelevant” properties, further
demonstrating the effectiveness of disentanglement
Supplementary 2.3: energy analysis of generated molecules. We show our model achieves
comparable and often superior molecular energy than the baselines. This shows our model
does not compromise the generation quality despite more challenging generative tasks
and higher model capacity.
Supplementary 2.5: conformer generation by only updating the 3D coordinates. We show
the semantics control slightly improves the validity of generation

We have demonstrated the uniqueness and importance of our work in the cover letter, but
we would also like to further emphasize that:
1. Unlike previous studies such as MolDiff, the focus of our work is a novel one: how to

compositions and properties simultaneously remains unexplored. For example, existing
works could generate molecules “with high QED”, “with two halogens”, “with good water

three at once remains a challenge and requires large amounts of labeled data. In our work,
we only use a small labelled dataset (10% of the training data) for the manipulation of up to

indicate a well-regularized latent space and a strong semantic guidance of the generation.

work are surprisingly simple: through constrained quadratic optimization, classifier back-
propagation and linear interpolation. Despite that, our model still achieves significantly
superior results. Thus, we believe more specialized and effective methods for latent space
optimization would be directly applied to our framework and further enhance the results.

Thanks for pointing this out. We want to note that the “disentanglement” in the context of
controlled generation refers to manipulating the disentangled features that relate to the
multiple and sometimes conflicting objectives, respectively. It is also worth mentioning
that many of the molecular properties are correlated (especially the RDKit descriptors in
our main experiments), but it is still practically important to minimize the “side effects”
during the molecular manipulation.
For example, to increase the molecule's solubility, one manipulation approach is to
remove the halogens, but it is not the only viable solution. Without explicit control over
other properties, there is no guarantee which direction the modification will take. However,
as shown in Fig. 7, when the halogen number is explicitly controlled, the model will seek
“other modifications” that counteract the hydrophobicity of the halogen. This is an
example of the disentangled control: the model takes modification directions for each
property that do not interfere with each other.
Also, as many of the properties are correlated, it is hard to select a certain group of “other
properties” to evaluate. Thus, we evaluate the preservation of the “other properties”
through a higher-level metric of 2D and 3D Tanimoto similarity. As long as the composition
and shape of the molecule do not change drastically, we could assume that those
properties are mostly preserved. We have added a new supplementary figure showing that
certain properties, such as the number of halogens and asphericity, would not change
drastically unless explicitly changed.

The reason why it is not as visually separable as the other properties may be due to QED’s

Empirically, the claim of the successful manipulation of QED is backed by multiple
analyses of the real experimental results, including raw success counts and individual
case studies (direct QED score comparison between the manipulated and source
molecule). To provide a theoretical insight into the reason behind the success, our
manipulation method looks for a direction in the latent space that points towards higher
QED. Thus, as long as the QED values follow a well-regulated manifold, the chances of that
manipulation direction ending at a higher QED value would be high.
The “disentanglement” in QED manipulation is similar to that of SAS and LogP in Fig. 7,

We treat the one-hot vectors as multi-dimensional independent Gaussian distributions,

concerns: a discrete representation and categorical distribution could potentially improve
the generation quality, as shown in [2], [3]. However, for our controlled generation tasks
using DDIM, such a categorical model could not be easily inverted deterministically,
resulting in weaker controllability than a fully invertible, continuous model [4].
